params.title: VHF-DSC Equipment & Operation
params.subtitle: Channels and tolerances, front-panel controls, FM receivers and transmitters, DSC signals, antennas, and diagnosing common faults.

onScreen: Channels, controls, receivers, transmitters, DSC and antennas
scenes.narration: This lesson is all about the marine VHF-DSC radio: VHF for very high frequency, and DSC for digital selective calling. We'll cover its channels and frequency tolerances, its front-panel controls, and how its FM, or frequency modulation, receiver and transmitter work. Then the digital selective calling signal itself, and good antenna practice. Along the way, we'll diagnose common receiver and transmitter faults from their symptoms and test readings. Let's start with the channels.

onScreen: Channel 16, 156.800 MHz: voice calling and distress
Channels 10 and 11: 25 kHz either side of Channel 70
scenes.narration: Three channels matter most. Channel 16, 156.800 megahertz, is the voice calling and distress channel. Channel 70, 156.525 megahertz, is reserved for digital selective calling. And Channel 13, 156.650 megahertz, is the bridge-to-bridge channel. Marine VHF channels are spaced 25 kilohertz apart. So Channel 70 sits exactly halfway between Channel 10, at 156.500 megahertz, and Channel 11, at 156.550 megahertz, 25 kilohertz from each.

params.title: Duplex split and DSC tolerance
items: Duplex channels: transmit and receive frequencies are 4.6 MHz apart
Channel 26: ship transmits on 157.300 MHz, coast station on 161.900 MHz
DSC carrier frequency tolerance: 10 ppm (parts per million)
At 156.525 MHz: 156.525 MHz × 10×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1565 Hz either way

scenes.narration: Some channels are duplex: the ship and the coast station transmit on different frequencies, 4.6 megahertz apart. On Channel 26, ships transmit on 157.300 megahertz and the coast station on 161.900 megahertz. 161.900 minus 157.300 is 4.6 megahertz. Next, accuracy. The allowed frequency tolerance for the DSC carrier frequencies is 10 parts per million. At 156.525 megahertz, that's 156.525 megahertz times 10 parts per million, or about 1565 hertz either way.

params.title: Checking with a frequency counter
steps: 2 ppm counter: 8 ppm of 156.800 MHz ≈ 1254 Hz
5 ppm counter: 5 ppm of 157.200 MHz = 786 Hz
params.answer: All four readings are within legal tolerance

onScreen: 2 ppm counter: 8 ppm; 1242 Hz low and 1243 Hz high are legal
5 ppm counter: 5 ppm; 774 Hz high and 679 Hz low are legal
scenes.narration: When you check with a frequency counter, the counter's own error counts against you. Subtract its accuracy from the 10 parts per million limit, and a reading is certainly legal only if its offset fits inside what remains. With a 2 parts per million counter, 10 minus 2 leaves 8 parts per million: about 1254 hertz at 156.800 megahertz, and 1252 hertz at 156.525 megahertz. So 156,798.758 kilohertz, 1242 hertz low, and 156,526.243 kilohertz, 1243 hertz high, are legal. With a 5 parts per million counter, 10 minus 5 leaves 5 parts per million: about 784 hertz at 156.875 megahertz, and 786 hertz at 157.200 megahertz. So 156,875.774 kilohertz, 774 hertz high, and 157,199.321 kilohertz, 679 hertz low, are legal too. The exam prints two of these with a stray point where the comma belongs.

callouts.label: USA-INT switch: changes designated channels from duplex to simplex
Dual Watch: one receiver switching rapidly between Channel 16 and another
Squelch: standard on every VHF-DSC set
Power: 1 W on Low for short range, 25 W on High
Distress button under a red cover, plus Cancel: both standard

onScreen: Dual Watch: one receiver, switching between two channels
scenes.narration: Here's the front panel of a VHF-DSC transceiver. The USA-INT switch, short for U.S.A. or International, changes designated channels from duplex to simplex operation in U.S. waters; more on that in a moment. Dual Watch rapidly switches the radio's single receiver between two channels, usually Channel 16 and one other. It does not receive both at the same time. The squelch control is standard on VHF-DSC sets. FCC, or Federal Communications Commission, rules permit two power levels: 1 watt on Low Power and 25 watts on High Power. Use low power for short-range calls, such as harbor and bridge-to-bridge traffic. Finally, the Distress button, under its red cover, and the Cancel control are standard too.

params.title: USA-INT left on INT in U.S. waters

marks.label: Simplex frequency
marks.note: You transmit here; U.S. stations reply here

marks.label: 4.6 MHz higher
marks.note: Where INT mode listens: the reply is missed

onScreen: You transmit on the simplex frequency, and replies come back there
INT mode listens 4.6 MHz higher: replies missed
scenes.narration: Why does USA-INT matter? Some channels that are duplex under the international plan are used simplex in U.S. waters. That's why the switch changes them from duplex to simplex. Now suppose it's left on INT in U.S. waters. You transmit on the simplex frequency, and U.S. stations reply on that same frequency. But your radio is listening 4.6 megahertz higher, on the international duplex frequency. So on certain channels, your signals will be heard, but other stations' replies will not be heard.

params.title: Setting squelch, and the missing R.I.T.
items: For maximum sensitivity: just below the point where noise breaks through
Advance squelch only until background noise is just silenced
Turning it further blocks weak stations
R.I.T. (receiver incremental tuning) fine-tunes MF/HF single-sideband receivers
No R.I.T. on a VHF-DSC set; Distress, Cancel and Squelch are standard

onScreen: Squelch just below where noise breaks through
Advance only until noise is just silenced
scenes.narration: For maximum sensitivity, set the squelch just below the point where the noise breaks through. In practice, advance it only until the background noise is just silenced. Turning it any further blocks weak stations. Now a control you will not find on a VHF-DSC transceiver: R.I.T., or receiver incremental tuning. It fine-tunes MF and HF, medium and high frequency, single-sideband receivers. Distress, Cancel and Squelch, on the other hand, are standard on VHF-DSC sets.

params.title: Capture effect in an FM receiver

onScreen: Strong and weak signals on one channel
Limiter locks onto the stronger signal
Ratio detector: balance for best signal-to-noise
scenes.narration: Suppose two signals arrive on the same channel, one strong and one weak. Both pass through the IF, or intermediate frequency, amplifier to the limiter. The limiter and detector lock onto the stronger signal and suppress the weaker one, so only the stronger one reaches the audio. This is the capture effect: an FM receiver rejects all but the strongest signal on a channel. The detector here is a ratio detector. Its ratio arm balance control bridge is adjusted for improved signal-to-noise, because equalizing the two diode arms maximizes rejection of AM, or amplitude modulation, noise.

params.title: What a limiter does
labels: Input: amplitude varies with noise and fading
The frequency swings, which carry the information, pass through
A clean signal goes on to the detector

scenes.narration: A properly adjusted limiter maintains a constant output amplitude with a varying input amplitude. The signal coming in rises and falls with noise and fading. The limiter holds it to one steady level, like the trace you see here. The frequency swings, which carry the information in FM, pass straight through. So amplitude noise and fading are stripped off before the signal reaches the detector.

params.title: SINAD: measuring receiver sensitivity
steps: S = signal, N = noise, D = distortion
params.answer: 12 dB SINAD: the common FM sensitivity reference

onScreen: 12 dB SINAD: common FM sensitivity reference
scenes.narration: Receiver sensitivity is often measured with SINAD, short for signal plus noise and distortion. SINAD is the sum of the signal, noise and distortion, divided by the sum of the noise and distortion. It's usually expressed in decibels. And 12 decibels SINAD is the common reference for FM receiver sensitivity.

params.title: Quieting: how much signal it takes
items: Normal VHF marine receiver: 10 dB of quieting with about 1 µV at the antenna input
Needing 5 or 10 µV for that means poor sensitivity
Full quieting: the signal is strong enough to completely quiet the background noise
Full quieting describes signal strength, not a squelch setting

onScreen: 10 dB quieting with about 1 µV: normal
Full quieting: background noise completely quieted
scenes.narration: Another sensitivity check is quieting: how far a signal pushes down the receiver's background noise. A normal VHF marine receiver reaches 10 decibels of quieting with about 1 microvolt at the antenna input. If it needs 5 or 10 microvolts to get there, its sensitivity is poor. Full quieting means the received signal is strong enough to completely quiet the receiver background noise. That describes the signal's strength. It is not a squelch setting.

blocks.label: Mixer
blocks.note: Local oscillator beat makes the IF: normal

blocks.label: Limiter
blocks.note: A stronger signal can capture a weak one

onScreen: RF amplifier, mixer, IF amplifier, limiter
Mixer: local oscillator beat is normal
PLL synthesizer unlocked: won't stay on channel
scenes.narration: Here's the receiver chain: the RF, or radio frequency, amplifier, the mixer, the IF amplifier and the limiter, with the synthesizer feeding the mixer, and at the end the speaker, driven by the audio amplifier after the detector and squelch. First fault: the receiver cannot stay tuned to the desired channel. The frequency synthesizer's phase-locked loop, or PLL, output has become unlocked. Don't blame the local oscillator beating with the incoming signal to make an IF; that's normal operation. Second: a weak signal is lost while a stronger one is on the channel. The receiver is working. The stronger signal suppresses the weak one at the limiter stage, by capture effect.

params.title: Fails to receive: zero volts, good fuse

callouts.label: Radio fails to receive nearby stations
DC line to ground: zero volts
Fuse on the ohmmeter: zero ohms, so it's intact
A crowbar circuit shut off the supply to prevent an over current condition

onScreen: Crowbar circuit prevented an over current condition
scenes.narration: A radio fails to receive nearby stations. A voltmeter between the positive side of its DC, or direct current, line and ground reads zero volts. But the fuse reads zero ohms on an ohmmeter, so the fuse is intact. That rules out a blown fuse as the reason for the missing voltage. Instead, a crowbar circuit has shut off the supply, preventing an over current condition that might damage the radio.

params.title: No audio, and the squelch does nothing
items: Symptom: no audible speaker output, and the squelch control has no effect
So not even noise is reaching the speaker
RF, mixer or local oscillator faults would still leave noise audible
Suspect a defective AF amplifier…
…or an activated Push-To-Talk circuit: keying mutes the receiver

onScreen: No audio, squelch has no effect
Not even noise reaches the speaker
Front-end faults would still leave noise
scenes.narration: Here's one to reason through. The speaker gives no audible output, and the squelch control has no effect. Opening the squelch should at least let noise through, so not even noise is reaching the speaker. That rules out the front end: if the RF amplifier, the mixer or the local oscillator had failed, you'd still hear noise from the stages after them. So look near the end of the chain. The AF, or audio frequency, amplifier may be defective. Or the transmitter's Push-To-Talk, or PTT, circuit may be activated, because keying the transmitter mutes the receiver.

callouts.label: Probe the output of each AF amplifier stage in turn
The scope displays the AC audio signal
Clean audio: that stage is fine, move on
The stage where clean audio first turns distorted is the fault

onScreen: First distorted stage is the fault
scenes.narration: To isolate distortion in the audio output, use an oscilloscope. Probe the output of each AF amplifier stage in turn, and display the AC, or alternating current, signal there. While the trace stays clean, those stages are fine, so move on to the next one. The stage where clean audio first turns distorted is the faulty one.

params.title: Readings and what they cause
rows: DC line reads 9.6, not 12.8 to 13.8 V
75 Ω RG-59/U → 50 Ω RG-8/U or LMR-400
Better match, less loss: no sensitivity loss

onScreen: 9.6 on the DC line: significant sensitivity loss
RG-59/U to RG-8/U or LMR-400: no loss
scenes.narration: Now some readings and their results. A voltmeter between the positive side of the DC line and ground reads 9.6, instead of the normal 12.8 to 13.8 volts. That starves the receiver stages and may cause a significant loss in sensitivity. Replacing 75-ohm RG-59/U coax with 50-ohm RG-8/U or LMR-400 Ultraflex cable does not cause a loss. It improves the match and cuts line loss. Noisy, crackling operation points to a defective potentiometer in the audio frequency amplifier stage, such as a worn volume control. An open coupling transformer winding would not crackle; it would kill the audio instead.

params.title: Finding the minimum discernible signal
items: Set a signal generator to the receiver frequency
Start near zero output
Watch an audio voltmeter at the AF output
Increase the output until the audio voltmeter shows a 3-dB increase
There, signal plus noise is twice the noise

onScreen: Signal generator on the receiver frequency
Audio voltmeter at the AF output
Signal plus noise is twice the noise
scenes.narration: To find a receiver's minimum discernible signal, set a signal generator to the receiver frequency. Start near zero output. Connect an audio voltmeter at the AF output. Then increase the generator output until the audio voltmeter shows a 3-decibel increase. At that point, signal plus noise is twice the noise, and that generator level is the minimum discernible signal.

params.title: Quick field test: NOAA weather broadcasts

scenes.narration: Here's a quick field test that works in many U.S. ports. Tune the receiver to 162.550, 162.400 or 162.475 megahertz, and listen for National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, broadcasts. If you hear them, the receiver is working. Why not just transmit and listen to yourself? Because a radio cannot monitor its own transmission.

callouts.label: Transistor emitter-base low both ways: shorted junction, faulty
Diode: low one way, high reversed: normal
Good fuse: zero ohms: normal
Ceramic bypass capacitor: infinite ohms: normal
100K-ohm bias resistor: same voltage at both leads = fault

onScreen: Diode low one way, high reversed: normal
Ceramic bypass capacitor infinite ohms: normal
100K-ohm bias resistor, same voltage both ends: fault
scenes.narration: Ohmmeter checks first. A transistor that shows low resistance between emitter and base, even with the test leads reversed, is faulty: the junction is shorted. Compare the normal readings. A diode reads low one way and high when reversed. A good fuse reads zero ohms. A ceramic bypass capacitor reads infinite ohms. Now a voltage check. In a bias circuit, a working 100 kilohm resistor carries current, so there's a voltage drop across it. If you read the same voltage between each lead and ground, that indicates a fault.

params.title: Deviation and emission type
items: Maximum allowable deviation: 5 kHz (±5 kHz for 16K0G3E voice)
More deviation spreads the signal toward adjacent channels
G3E: the most common emission for shipboard VHF-DSC transceivers
G = phase modulation · 3 = one channel of analog information · E = telephony

onScreen: Phase modulation, one analog channel, telephony
scenes.narration: The maximum allowable deviation of a marine VHF transmitter is 5 kilohertz: plus or minus 5 kilohertz for 16K0G3E voice. More deviation spreads the signal toward the adjacent channels. That designator ends in G3E, the most common emission for shipboard VHF-DSC transceivers. G means phase modulation. 3 means a single channel of analog information. And E means telephony, which is voice.

The modulation index is the maximum carrier deviation divided by the maximum modulation frequency: m equals delta f over f sub m. With 5 kilohertz of deviation and a 2.5 kilohertz tone, m equals 5 divided by 2.5, which is 2. If the modulation index is set to less than 1 to 1, the transmitter is undermodulated, and the result is unusually low level transmit audio.

onScreen: Sideband pairs at multiples of the modulating frequency
Many sidebands, not one or two
scenes.narration: A VHF FM transmitter does not make just one or two sidebands. It makes many. Around the carrier, the sidebands come in pairs at multiples of the modulating frequency: one pair at plus and minus f sub m, another at plus and minus 2 f sub m, and more beyond. Their amplitudes follow Bessel functions of the modulation index. The significant ones fit within the 16 kilohertz necessary bandwidth.

blocks.label: Pre-emphasis
blocks.note: Boosts high audio 6 dB per octave

blocks.label: De-emphasis
blocks.note: Same cut: flat audio, less noise

onScreen: Pre-emphasis: high audio up 6 dB per octave
Noise picked up on the way
scenes.narration: Pre-emphasis boosts the higher modulation frequencies by 6 decibels per octave before transmitting. On the way to the receiver, the signal picks up noise, and the high-frequency noise is the most noticeable. The receiver's de-emphasis reduces those higher frequencies by the same amount. That cuts the high-frequency noise while keeping the audio flat.

onScreen: Meter between the radio and the antenna coax
scenes.narration: To measure the antenna system's SWR, or standing wave ratio, insert an SWR meter between the VHF radio and the coax connected to the antenna. Set an unused channel, activate the Push-To-Talk circuit, and read the value. A directional wattmeter goes in the same place, between the transmitter and the coax. Activate PTT and observe the forward and reflected power. Don't settle for a radio check on Channel 16. And don't measure into an artificial antenna, which tests only the radio, or a disconnected line, which reflects everything.

params.title: SWR from forward and reflected power
params.answer: An SWR of 1.5 to 1.0 is normal

scenes.narration: From the wattmeter's two readings, you can work out the SWR. It equals 1 plus the square root of P sub r over P sub f, divided by 1 minus the square root of P sub r over P sub f. P sub f is the forward power, and P sub r is the reflected power. An SWR of 1.5 to 1.0 is normal for a working antenna system.

params.title: Reading the power meter
rows: 1 W on LOW, 8.5 W on HIGH at +12.8 vdc
Low, but within FCC specs: 8 W to 25 W
Nearly zero RF output on HIGH, all channels
SWR protection engaged to protect the PA
SWR of 1.5 to 1.0, or a 50-ohm load

onScreen: 8.5 W on High: low but within FCC specifications
Nearly zero output on High: SWR protection engaged
scenes.narration: Now read the symptoms. A radio can't contact nearby stations. The wattmeter shows 1 watt on Low and 8.5 watts on High, with plus 12.8 volts DC applied. The high power output is low, but it's still within FCC specifications: at least 8 watts and no more than 25. So the problem lies elsewhere. Next, the radio otherwise works normally, but it produces nearly zero RF output in high power mode on all channels. The SWR protection circuit has engaged to prevent damage to the Power Amplifier, or PA. A 1.5 to 1.0 SWR or a 50-ohm load is normal and would not cause this.

params.title: When the radio won't transmit
items: VCO (voltage controlled oscillator) failure in the synthesizer…
…shows up as an out-of-lock condition in the Phase Locked Loop
Many radios then inhibit transmit
Receives but can't transmit: a failed component in the PTT circuit
The radio enters transmit only when the PTT line is activated

onScreen: VCO failure: PLL out of lock
Receive works, no transmit: PTT circuit
Transmit only when the PTT line is activated
scenes.narration: Two reasons a radio won't transmit. First, voltage controlled oscillator, or VCO, failure in the synthesizer. It shows up as an out-of-lock condition in the phase-locked loop, and many radios then inhibit transmit. Second, a radio that works in receive mode but cannot transmit. Receive works, so power and the receiver are fine; the trouble is in getting into transmit. The radio enters transmit only when the PTT line is activated, so the most likely cause is a failed component in the Push-To-Talk circuit.

A wattmeter reads 25 watts forward and 1.5 watts reflected. Is that OK? First find gamma, the reflection coefficient: the square root of P sub r over P sub f. The square root of 1.5 over 25 is about 0.245. Then SWR equals 1 plus 0.245, divided by 1 minus 0.245, or about 1.65 to 1. That shows proper operation. Compare two bad readings: 27.5 watts forward exceeds the legal limit, and 25 watts reflected means nothing reaches the antenna.

params.title: Checking transmitter stages with a SPECAN

blocks.label: Inductive probe
blocks.note: Input and output of RF transmitter stages

onScreen: Inductive probe on the RF transmitter stages
scenes.narration: To evaluate transmitter stages with a spectrum analyzer, or SPECAN, protect the analyzer. Switch the radio to LOW power. Connect it through an in-line attenuator set to maximum attenuation, and then to the SPECAN. Use an inductive probe to evaluate the signals at the input and output of the RF transmitter stages.

params.title: More transmitter faults
rows: 25 W output, but no modulation heard
Under 1 W on HIGH with 12.8 vdc applied
Insufficient bias voltage to the PA stage

onScreen: 25 W, no modulation: open microphone cable or connector
Under 1 W on High: insufficient PA bias
scenes.narration: Three more fault patterns. The wattmeter shows a full 25 watts on High, but an external receiver hears no modulation. What still works? The carrier, so the PTT circuit is fine: a PTT fault would prevent any output at all. Suspect an open connection in the microphone cable or connector. Next, less than 1 watt on High with a nominal 12.8 volts DC applied. The supply is fine, so the bias voltage to the PA stage may be insufficient, and the PA transistor barely conducts. Finally, modulation in excess of 150 percent causes distortion in the modulator stage. 100 percent is the 5 kilohertz maximum deviation, so 150 percent swings the carrier about 7.5 kilohertz.

params.title: Dummy load, or artificial antenna
items: Tests RF power output without emitting a signal on the air
A non-inductive 50 Ω resistor
Absorbs the transmitter's power as heat

onScreen: Tests RF output off the air
scenes.narration: To test the RF power output without emitting a signal on the air, connect a dummy load, also called an artificial antenna. It's a non-inductive 50-ohm resistor that absorbs the transmitter's power as heat. Remember, though: it tests only the radio, not the antenna system.

VHF-DSC uses a frequency shift between 1300 and 2100 hertz, on a 1700 hertz sub-carrier: that's 1700, plus or minus 400 hertz. These tones modulate the transmitter on Channel 70. The modulation rate is 1200 baud, with an index of modulation of 2.0, plus or minus 10 percent. MF and HF DSC, by contrast, run at only 100 baud.

params.title: Time diversity: why 33⅓ ms
steps: Each character is sent (DX), then repeated (RX)
4 other characters come between the two copies
Each character is 10 bits, sent at 1200 baud

scenes.narration: VHF-DSC sends every character twice, a technique called time diversity, and the reception interval is 4 times 10 bits, divided by 1200 bits per second. Here's where that comes from. Each character is first sent as DX, then repeated as RX. Between the two copies come 4 other characters. Each character is 10 bits long, sent at 1200 bits per second. So the time diversity reception interval is 33 and a third milliseconds.

params.title: DSC radio check and the MMSI

callouts.label: DSC menu: select TEST
Enter the coast station's MMSI, not its call letters, then send
Red cover: the distress alert button, never for a test
MMSI locked after one entry: the manufacturer must clear it

onScreen: Enter the coast station's MMSI and send
scenes.narration: To make a DSC radio check with a coast station, select the DSC menu item TEST. Enter the coast station's MMSI, or Maritime Mobile Service Identity, number, and send the test. DSC addresses stations by MMSI, not by call letters. And don't touch the button under the red cover: it sends a distress alert. What if the radio already has an MMSI and won't accept a new one? Most DSC radios lock the MMSI after one entry and have no user reset. Contact the manufacturer to clear the MMSI memory.

params.title: Voltmeter on an outgoing DSC data stream
labels: Outgoing DSC message: a fast-switching data stream
Voltmeter: fluctuating reading from 0 to 2 volts DC
The data switches faster than the meter can follow

onScreen: Faster than the meter can follow
scenes.narration: One more DSC test. Put a voltmeter on a DSC circuit while it sends an outgoing message data stream. The voltmeter shows a fluctuating reading, from 0 to 2 volts DC. Why fluctuating? The data switches faster than the meter can follow. So you won't see a steady voltage, and you won't see an absence of voltage.

params.title: Length of a temporary VHF antenna

scenes.narration: Need a temporary VHF marine antenna? Make it about 18 inches long: a quarter wave. The quarter-wave formula is L, in feet, equals 234 divided by the frequency in megahertz. At 156.8 megahertz, L equals 234 divided by 156.8, or about 1.49 feet. That's about 18 inches.

callouts.label: Collinear array: phased elements, omnidirectional pattern
Half-wave elements stacked end to end: up to 9 dB gain
High gain: the flat beam tilts as a small boat rolls, so signals drop out
Base loading coil reads shorted on an ohmmeter
May be normal if shunt fed: the coil grounds the radiator at DC

onScreen: High gain: dropout in severe weather on small craft
Normal for a shunt fed antenna
scenes.narration: A VHF collinear array is an antenna with phased elements and an omnidirectional radiation pattern. Stacking half-wave elements end to end gives it up to 9 decibels of gain. High gain has a disadvantage, though. On small craft in severe weather, the narrow, flattened beam tilts toward the sky or the water as the boat rolls, and the signal drops out. Now an ohmmeter check: the base loading coil of a masthead antenna appears shorted. That may be normal for a well working shunt fed antenna system, because the coil connects the radiator to ground at DC.

params.title: Coax cable and connectors
rows: Much lower loss: best for a long run
PL-259 plug into an SO-239 socket

onScreen: RG-8/U: best for a long run
UHF connector: PL-259 plug, SO-239 socket
scenes.narration: For a long transmission line run, RG-8/U is the most appropriate coax. It's a large 50-ohm cable, with much lower loss than RG-58/U or RG-174/U. RG-59/U is a 75-ohm cable, so it mismatches the radio. And the most common coax connector on VHF transceivers is the UHF, or ultra high frequency, type: an SO-239 socket on the radio mates with a PL-259 plug on the coax.
